Indicator: 18.2 Value of subsidies and other incentives harmful to biodiversity
Comments: A national analytical screening conducted under the UNDP–BIOFIN subsidy repurposing methodology assessed government subsidies and incentives during 2020–2024. The rapid assessment identified approximately MNT 1.96 trillion (equivalent to approximately USD 551.2 million at 1 USD = 3,557 MNT ) in subsidies across agriculture, energy, transport, infrastructure and urban development sectors that may be harmful or potentially harmful to biodiversity. Within agriculture alone, 10 major subsidy instruments accounted for MNT 552.2 billion during 2020–2024. The assessment identified 50 subsidy instruments in total: 29 classified as clearly harmful (24 in agriculture), 21 classified as potentially harmful (16 in agriculture). These figures represent cumulative estimates for 2020–2024 and are derived from national fiscal data screened under BIOFIN methodology. They have not yet been formally adopted as official harmful subsidy accounting in national budget statistics. Annual disaggregated values are not available.

Target: NT13. By 2030, establish systems to monitor and transparently report the impacts, risks, and outcomes of business activities regarding biodiversity.
Indicator: D.3 Private funding (domestic and international) on conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity and ecosystems
Footnote: In analyzing private sector biodiversity-related expenditures, data collection focused on the Top 100 companies identified by the Mongolian National Chamber of Commerce and Industry, as well as major mining companies. The combined revenues of Mongolia’s Top 100 enterprises account for approximately 70 percent of national GDP, indicating a high level of representativeness relative to the population of approximately 87,000 active legal entities as of 2024. Data on biodiversity-related expenditures were collected through a review of corporate social responsibility and sustainability reports, as well as publicly available information disclosed through media sources. Where such information was not available, standardized questionnaires were distributed to enterprises to collect data on biodiversity- and environment-related expenditures.
